name: Logistic Regression
short_description: Models class probabilities using a linear combination of features passed through a sigmoid function.
intuition: Draws a straight linear decision boundary between classes, converting raw scores into calibrated probabilities (0% to 100%).
step_by_step_working: Standardize continuous feature inputs.
Calculate linear log-odds: z = w^T * x + b.
Pass through sigmoid curve to yield probability p = 1 / (1 + exp(-z)).
Compute binary cross-entropy loss against true labels.
Optimize weights iteratively using L-BFGS or gradient descent.

parameters.name: C
parameters.description: Inverse of regularization strength; smaller values specify stronger regularization.

parameters.name: max_iter
parameters.description: Maximum number of iterations taken for the solvers to converge.

advantages: Fast, stable, and outputs well-calibrated probabilities.
Highly interpretable through odds ratios.
Resistant to overfitting when regularized with appropriate C.
limitations: Cannot model non-linear boundaries without manual feature engineering.
Can struggle when classes have complex multi-modal distributions.
when_to_use: When a fast, explainable baseline is required.
When calibrated probabilities are needed to set custom decision thresholds.
when_to_avoid: When decision boundaries are known to be non-linear.
python_snippet:
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
model = LogisticRegression(C=1.0, max_iter=200, random_state=42)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred = model.predict(X_test)
code_explanation: Fits a regularized logistic regression model and computes class predictions.

name: K-Nearest Neighbors Classifier
short_description: Non-parametric lazy learner classifying query instances by taking a majority vote of the K nearest neighbors.
intuition: Looks at the K closest training examples in feature space. If 4 out of 5 closest points are Class A, it classifies the new point as Class A.
step_by_step_working: Standardize all feature coordinates to eliminate scale bias.
Store training feature vectors in memory (no explicit training phase).
For a new query point, compute Euclidean distance to every training sample.
Sort samples by distance and identify the K smallest distances.
Assign the most frequent class label among the K neighbors as the prediction.

parameters.name: n_neighbors
parameters.description: Number of neighbors to use by default for k-neighbors queries.

parameters.name: weights
parameters.description: Weight function used in prediction ('uniform' or 'distance').

advantages: Naturally handles multi-class problems and irregular non-linear decision regions.
No underlying assumptions about data distribution.
limitations: Inference slows down on large datasets ($O(n \cdot d)$ per prediction).
Degrades severely with high-dimensional data (curse of dimensionality).
use_cases: Handwriting recognition and digit optical character classification.
User recommendation based on neighbor similarity.
when_to_use: When dataset has modest sample size (<50k rows) and low feature dimensions (<30).
When non-linear decision boundaries exist and fast training is needed.
when_to_avoid: When dataset is huge or sub-millisecond inference latency is required.
python_snippet:
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
model = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5, weights='uniform')
model.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)
y_pred = model.predict(X_test_scaled)
code_explanation: Fits KNN with 5 neighbors. Features must be standardized so distance metrics are not biased by unit magnitude.

name: Decision Tree Classifier
short_description: Recursively partitions feature space using Gini impurity or entropy to create hierarchical if-else decision rules.
intuition: Plays a game of 20 questions with your data, picking questions that best separate classes into pure subgroups.
step_by_step_working: Compute initial Gini impurity at current node.
Evaluate all candidate feature thresholds to find the split minimizing weighted child Gini impurity.
Split training samples into left and right subsets.
Recurse until max depth, minimum sample counts, or pure leaves are attained.
For inference, navigate down the tree and output the majority class at the terminal leaf.

parameters.name: max_depth
parameters.description: The maximum depth of the tree.

parameters.name: min_samples_split
parameters.description: The minimum number of samples required to split an internal node.

advantages: Completely interpretable and visualizable as a flowchart.
No feature scaling or transformation required.
Handles categorical and numerical features effortlessly.
limitations: High variance: slight changes in training data produce completely different trees.
Prone to severe overfitting if depth is unconstrained.
when_to_use: When business stakeholders require clear, visual decision paths.
When speed and simplicity take precedence over complex ensembles.
when_to_avoid: When highest possible classification accuracy on complex datasets is needed.
python_snippet:
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
model = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=5, min_samples_split=2, random_state=42)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred = model.predict(X_test)
code_explanation: Trains a pruned decision tree classifier capped at depth 5.

name: Random Forest Classifier
short_description: Ensemble of diverse decision trees built on bootstrap data slices and random feature subsets with majority voting.
intuition: Combines votes from 100 independently trained trees. Even if individual trees make mistakes on certain patterns, their collective majority vote is remarkably accurate and reliable.
step_by_step_working: Draw B bootstrap datasets (sampling with replacement) from the training data.
For each bootstrap sample, build an unpruned decision tree.
At every internal node split, randomly choose a subset of features (typically sqrt(p)).
During prediction, pass query point through all B trees.
Aggregate individual tree votes and return the class with the most votes.

parameters.name: n_estimators
parameters.description: The number of trees in the forest.

advantages: One of the most accurate and reliable general-purpose tabular classification models.
Highly resilient to overfitting and outliers.
Computes informative feature importance scores.
limitations: Large model size and memory footprint.
Cannot be directly visualized as a simple flowchart like a single tree.
use_cases: Customer churn prediction and retention modeling.
Disease diagnosis from clinical health profiles.
when_to_use: When working with tabular data and seeking superior predictive performance without extensive tuning.
when_to_avoid: When extreme low-latency prediction on microcontrollers is needed.
python_snippet:
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, max_depth=10, random_state=42)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred = model.predict(X_test)
code_explanation: Builds 100 trees in parallel and aggregates votes for robust classification.

name: Gaussian Naive Bayes
short_description: Probabilistic classifier applying Bayes theorem under the strong naive assumption that features are conditionally independent.
intuition: Calculates the probability of each class given the observed features by multiplying individual feature probabilities together, assuming each feature clue is completely independent of the others.
step_by_step_working: Calculate prior class probabilities P(y) from training label frequencies.
Compute mean and variance for each feature conditioned on each class.
For a new query point, evaluate the Gaussian probability density of each feature for each class.
Multiply prior probability by feature likelihoods for each candidate class.
Select the class with the maximum posterior probability.

parameters.name: var_smoothing
parameters.description: Portion of the largest variance of all features that is added to variances for calculation stability.

advantages: Extremely fast training and prediction with minimal memory overhead.
Performs surprisingly well even on small datasets and high-dimensional text.
Not sensitive to irrelevant features.
limitations: The 'naive' assumption of complete feature independence is rarely true in real life.
Outputs extreme probability estimates near 0 or 1.
use_cases: Spam email detection and text sentiment analysis.
when_to_use: When dealing with small datasets or text/bag-of-words classifications.
When training speed must be virtually instantaneous.
when_to_avoid: When features have strong mutual correlations and dependencies.
python_snippet:
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB
model = GaussianNB()
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred = model.predict(X_test)
code_explanation: Computes class priors and Gaussian feature likelihoods for instant classification.

name: Support Vector Machine Classifier (SVC)
short_description: Finds the optimal separating hyperplane that maximizes the geometric margin between classes in high-dimensional space.
intuition: Draws a wide highway between two classes. The margin width is maximized so that the closest points (support vectors) are as far from the center line as possible, giving strong generalization.
step_by_step_working: Standardize all feature coordinates to unit scale (essential for SVM).
Formulate the convex quadratic optimization problem.
Identify the critical support vectors along the margin boundaries.
Solve for dual Lagrange multipliers alpha_i.
Classify new query points using sign(w^T * phi(x) + b).

parameters.name: C
parameters.description: Regularization parameter. Strength of margin penalty; smaller C allows wider margins with more margin violations.

parameters.name: kernel
parameters.description: Specifies the kernel type to be used in the algorithm.

advantages: Effective in high-dimensional spaces, even where feature count exceeds sample count ($p > n$).
Memory efficient because decision function uses only a small subset of training points (support vectors).
RBF kernel models complex non-linear boundaries gracefully.
limitations: Training scales quadratically with sample size ($O(n^2)$ to $O(n^3)$); slow on datasets > 50,000 rows.
when_to_use: When dataset has high dimensions and clean margins.
When training dataset has fewer than 20,000 rows.
when_to_avoid: On very large datasets (>50,000 samples) where training becomes prohibitively slow.
python_snippet:
from sklearn.svm import SVC
model = SVC(C=1.0, kernel='rbf', random_state=42)
model.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)
y_pred = model.predict(X_test_scaled)
code_explanation: Trains a support vector classifier with an RBF kernel. Input data must be standardized.

name: Gradient Boosting Classifier
short_description: Sequentially builds an ensemble of shallow decision trees that minimize cross-entropy loss via gradient descent.
intuition: Builds a sequence of trees where each new tree is trained specifically to correct the classification errors and probability gaps made by all earlier trees.
step_by_step_working: Initialize model with log-odds of positive class.
Calculate negative gradient pseudo-residuals (difference between true label and predicted probability).
Train a shallow decision tree to fit the pseudo-residuals.
Update ensemble log-odds predictions scaled by learning rate eta.
Repeat for n_estimators iterations.
Pass final accumulated log-odds through sigmoid to produce probabilities.

parameters.name: n_estimators
parameters.description: The number of boosting stages to perform.

parameters.name: learning_rate
parameters.description: Learning rate shrinks the contribution of each tree.

parameters.name: max_depth
parameters.description: Maximum depth of the individual regression estimators.

advantages: Industry-leading classification accuracy on tabular datasets.
Optimizes directly for classification metrics and subtle edge cases.
Built-in feature importance evaluation.
limitations: Sequential training makes it slower than parallel Random Forests.
Requires careful tuning of learning rate and tree depth to prevent overfitting.
use_cases: Search ranking and ad click prediction.
Credit risk scoring and churn prevention.
when_to_use: When predictive accuracy is the top metric of success.
when_to_avoid: When training compute time is strictly limited.
When data has massive noise and mislabeled targets.
python_snippet:
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingClassifier
model = GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=100, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=3, random_state=42)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred = model.predict(X_test)
code_explanation: Fits a sequence of 100 boosted trees with learning_rate=0.1, optimizing cross-entropy loss.
